articles.title: Forgotten Island review – best friends forever trapped in frantic DreamWorks animation
articles.summary: This over-controlled adventure never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life. Frantically and even stroboscopically over-energised, this big new movie from DreamWorks about best friends for ever seems to me another example of exhausting AI-type content production in animation.
body: The story, weirdly reminiscent of The Hangover of all things, is set in the Philippines in the pre-social media 90s. Jo, voiced by R&B star HER, is a lonely and super-imaginative teen always in trouble at school; like Moana she has a wise grandma who guides her to her ancestral destiny and has captivated Jo with stories of her culture and identity – stories of the forgotten island of Nakali. Jo makes friends with similarly lonely Raissa (Liza Soberano) who like Jo is smart but with a much more focused sense of academic discipline.

This Hangover-style amnesia facilitates a quest narrative, in the course of which they meet a goofy pal in the form of a wacky shapeshifting dog called Raww (Dave Franco) and a scary batibat, or memory demon, resembling Jabba the Hutt called Batiba (Jenny Slate) to whom they may have to surrender precious memories in return for freedom. They also encounter the terrifying figure of Manang (Lea Salonga) who, like Batiba may have relatable vulnerabilities that we don’t yet appreciate. And so it continues, developing and resolving with algorithmic efficiency. It leaves you with a strange sense of emptiness.
points: This over-controlled adventure never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life.
Frantically and even stroboscopically over-energised, this big new movie from DreamWorks about best friends for ever seems to me another example of exhausting AI-type content production in animation.

articles.title: ‘The Eternaut’ Star Ricardo Darín on Argentina’s Resilience: ‘We’re Like Peter Sellers in ‘The Party,’ the Bugler Who Never Dies’
articles.summary: The premise of Argentina’s Ricardo Darin’s latest feature, “Therapy Done Right” (Lo dejamos acá”), world premiering at the San Sebastian Festival, is deceptively simple: A pragmatic psychoanalyst loses faith in conventional methods and starts pushing the boundaries with his patients.
body: Ricardo, you play the psychoanalyst who rejects an award at the onset, stating that Argentina has the largest number of psychoanalysts in the world and yet the percentage of Argentineans with some form of mental health issue has doubled. Is this a fact?

Yes, and I think it has something to do with the mix of cultures that shaped Argentina – Italians, Spaniards, Jews, Arabs, Germans… – really, a bit of everything. And I think that’s part of where it comes from. Argentina also embraced psychoanalysis a long time ago, and it’s worked for us. In many ways, it’s worked really well.

Everyone has mental health issues. A lot of people around the world do – they just don’t realize it. They think there’s something else causing it. I think it’s worth clarifying that, because otherwise it might give the impression that Argentinians are the only ones with mental health problems. That’s not the case.

But I also know there are more psychoanalysts in Argentina. There are a lot of psychoanalysts compared to other countries. Why is that? Nobody really knows. Because people have been drawn to studying it at university. Argentina has some very good universities for psychology and sociology.

articles.title: ‘200 Lives, Paco Rabal,’ Told in the Spanish Screen Legend’s Own Voice, Boarded by Latido Films
articles.summary: SAN SEBASTIAN, Spain – Paco Rabal worked with Luis Buñuel, Michelangelo Antonioni and Carlos Saura, made more than 200 films and built a career spanning Spain, France, Italy and Mexico. In “200 Lives, Paco Rabal,” the Spanish screen legend gets one more role: Narrator of his own life.
body: “Paco Rabal was and remains one of Spain’s and Europe’s top leading actors,” says Latido Films managing director Antonio Saura. “His versatility gave him innumerable recognitions, including a Cannes best actor award.”
But it is the personal material, Saura argues, that provides the sales proposition with another dimension.

“Here we find his life was as exciting as his talent, and listening to him narrate it, thanks to the amazing discovery of some self-recorded tapes, brings us a new perspective of his art and his life.”
For Benítez, the challenge was to peer behind Francisco Rabal, the internationally celebrated actor, and find Paco, the boy from rural Murcia.

articles.title: San Sebastian’s Creative Investors’ Conference: 10 Takeaways From AI to ‘Obsession,’ YouTube and Why International Movies Could Dominate the Oscars
articles.summary: It wasn’t just a sea breeze and late summer sun which brought a sense of new airs and targeted optimism blowing through the San Sebastian’s 2026 Creative Investors’ Conference.
body: For four years, CIC, co-organized with CAA Media Finance, has insisted on upsides and opportunities in drastic post-COVID and post-peak TV downturn.

That said, the market at large in TV sell belabors at 75% of peak TV levels, as Ampere Analysis points out. Huge problems in key markets, moreover, remain. One case in point: In Christine Vachon’s lapidary phrase, U.S. independent production is “basically fucked up.”

“I think it’s a recovery; it’s a phenomenal result,” said Neon head of distribution Elissa Federoff at a key first day CIC panel, The New U.S. Landscape. “Every year since the pandemic, we have seen growth, and it’s been amazing to watch. “COVID happened, strikes happened, theater closures happened, and in that time, there has been a rise of a lot of other channels of entertainment, gaming, social platforms, streaming platforms. We’ve seen opportunities for new pathways during this point,” added Federoff, a major cheerleader for optimism at the Conference.

articles.title: Netflix’s ‘A Different World’ Is a Bold, Fun and Timely Reboot Centering the Uniqueness of Gen Z: TV Review
articles.summary: Thirty-nine years after the beloved NBC series premiered, Netflix is reopening the gates of the fictional, historically Black Hillman College with “A Different World.” Created by Felicia Pride and executive produced by Debbie Allen (who helmed the first version of the sitcom), the bold and…
body: For a show about Gen Z characters — and certainly as a reboot or continuation — “A Different World” knocks it out of the park. The single-camera dramedy captures the unique experience of attending an HBCU in the 21st century while addressing issues like the current federal government’s retaliatory agenda against Black Americans, alongside expected themes like love triangles and financial aid woes in college. However, the series moves so fast that even the most focused viewer is likely to get whiplash.

Still, this rushed pace doesn’t take away “A Different World”’s dynamism. The series connects the generations seamlessly, letting cherished characters from the original show float in and out of the new one while giving the new faces the platform they deserve. The show works perfectly well as a standalone, but knowing the lore and history behind “The Cosby Show” spinoff and even Whitley and Dwayne’s romance will undoubtedly allow those viewers a well-layered experience.

articles.title: Teen rocker Nene Royal becomes first Thai to win America's Got Talent
articles.summary: Her heavy metal performance trumped nine other finalists, including magicians and even a robot crew.
body: Nene Royal, a 16-year-old rocker, has been crowned the latest winner of America's Got Talent - making her the first ever Thai winner of the long-running talent show.
For the show's finals on Tuesday in California, Nene, whose real name is Rattikarn Amloy, performed a rendition of Seven Nation Army by American rock duo The White Stripes.
Her heavy metal performances trumped nine other finalists, including magician acts, canine performers and even a robot dance crew.

Many in Thailand are celebrating her win, with some saying they were proud that she had made it to "one of the biggest stages in the world". The Thai government has called her an "inspiration to anyone who dares to dream big".

articles.title: Harry Potter play producer says cost of living made two-part show 'impossible'
articles.summary: The London production, which has been running for 10 years, will reopen next month as a one-part show.
body: A Harry Potter And The Cursed Child producer has said the rising cost of living made it "literally impossible" to retain the play's original format in two parts.
The production has been cut down to a single three-hour show and is set to re-open in the West End next month.

"The cost of living has gone up 30-40% since the pandemic, including running shows," producer Sonia Friedman said in comments reported by media at a launch event. "The only way we could continue to run it as a two-parter would be by charging an amount for the tickets that would be unaffordable and inaccessible."
The two-part play, a sequel to JK Rowling's books, premiered in the West End in 2016 and closed on 20 September.

articles.title: ‘A Different World’ Review: Netflix College Comedy Takes a Beloved Classic Into a Lively New Era, With Charm and Smarts to Spare
articles.summary: Maleah Joi Moon stars as Deborah, face of a fresh generation of Hillman students, while Jasmine Guy and Kadeem Hardison reprise their leading roles from the original 'Cosby Show' spinoff.
body: In its first few episodes, Netflix ’s A Different World does not quite live up to its title.

It’s not until this A Different World begins to come out from under the shadow of its parent that it really starts to flourish — but then flourish it does, aided by an endearing young ensemble and smart, heartfelt storytelling. By the end of its first season, it not only cements itself as a worthwhile standard-bearer for its predecessor, but proves ready to leave a mark of its own.

As is typical for one of these many-decades-later brand extensions, our new protagonist is a literal descendant of the old protagonists. College freshman Deborah (pronounced Deh-BOH-rah, never “Debra,” and played by the irresistibly radiant Maleah Joi Moon) is the youngest daughter of Whitley (Jasmine Guy), now a cosmetics mogul, and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison), now the school provost. She’s also something of the family’s black sheep, the well-meaning but impulsive one who can’t seem to stop getting into trouble.

articles.title: Will.i.am backs campaign for Sir Tom Jones to return to The Voice
articles.summary: Sir Tom Jones, 86, has appeared as an on-off coach on the ITV show since 2012.
body: Will.i.am has endorsed a petition to have Sir Tom Jones reinstated on ITV's The Voice.
Sir Tom told his social media followers earlier this month that the broadcaster had "fired" him as a judge on the show.
The 86-year-old singer from Treforest, Rhondda Cynon Taf, has appeared as an on-off coach on the singing competition since it premiered in 2012.
Superfan Aaron Howlett, 50, from Kingston-upon-Hull, started the petition which has received more than 63,000 signatures from around the world.

articles.title: Federal judge delays ruling on White House media ban
articles.summary: During a roughly 45-minute hearing, a lawyer for CNN, Politico and MS NOW disputed Trump administration arguments that the ban was over national security concerns.
body: A federal judge has heard arguments between the Trump Administration and three news organisations over the decision to bar them from reporting inside White House grounds.

In a brief hearing in Washington on Wednesday, Judge Timothy Kelly weighed a request from CNN, Politico and MS NOW for a temporary restraining order to urgently restore White House passes to 78 reporters.

A lawyer for the media outlets said that the White House is falsely arguing that national security concerns justify the ban. A justice department lawyer said the president has the right to "exclude anyone he wants" from certain locations inside the White House.
The judge said he would come to a decision as soon as he could.

articles.title: Star Trek Is Officially Rewriting ‘Strange New Worlds’ Winning Formula for Season 5 [Exclusive]
articles.summary: Akiva Goldsman reveals regret over not bringing William Shatner to Strange New Worlds, while he and Henry Alonso Myers tease major Season 5 changes.
body: Editor's Note: This interview contains spoilers for the Season 4 finale of Star Trek: Strange New Worlds.

COLLIDER: Much of this episode is anchored in Uhura and Scotty's relationship, which is, I think, mentioned offhandedly in the movies, but I'm curious, what made you want to explore that dynamic for this finale?

HENRY ALONSO MYERS: Well, part of that was that there's a lot of stuff that they kind of got into later, I think, in the films that imply that there's a whole world of emotion that is not really explored throughout the series. It's one of the fun things that we've gotten to do on this show was give those characters some things to play that they didn't get to do in the original show, but that have been implied.

They had interesting chemistry. We wanted to find, you know, we were interested in, the romance between them, and also it's an important episode where she's exploring, trying to make a, you know, like a time travel adjustment, and these things are much better if you have some emotional core that you're trying to save at the heart of it. And I think that because we felt that was there in the movies, it was something we could dig in and reveal more specifically.
points: Akiva Goldsman reveals regret over not bringing William Shatner to Strange New Worlds, while he and Henry Alonso Myers tease major Season 5 changes.
